title: John Does 1, 2, 4, & 5 v. Seattle Police Dep't
questions: Public records requests were made regarding the activities of Seattle police officers on January 6, 2021. Are the officers entitled to a preliminary injunction preventing disclosure of the public records? Can they litigate under pseudonym? What is an agency's obligation when disclosure may implicate a third party's constitutional rights?

title: Brown v. Old Navy, LLC
questions: The Washington Commercial Electronic Mail Act (CEMA) prohibits the sending of commercial emails that "contain[] false or misleading information in the subject line." This case asks us to determine whether the statute prohibits the transmission of a commercial email with a subject line containing any false or misleading information, or if it only prohibits subject lines that conceal the email's commercial nature

title: State v. J.H.-M.
questions: Is a custody condition prohibiting "sexually explicit conduct" defined by RCW 9.68A.011(4) unconstitutionally vague?

title: Atkerson v. Dep’t of Child., Youth, & Fams.
questions: A child received a fatal injury a few weeks after the State opened a child abuse investigation. Washington State has immunized itself and its agents for "acts or omissions in emergent placement investigations of child abuse . . . unless the act or omission constitutes gross negligence. Emergent placement investigations are those conducted prior to a shelter care hearing under RCW 13.34.065." RCW 4.24.595. This immunity "include[s], but [is] not limited to, any determination to leave a child with a parent . . . or to return a child to a parent." RCW 4.24.595. The court must decide whether this immunity applied in this case. The court must also decide whether the trial court erred in excluding one of the State's expert witnesses, a retired trial judge

title: State v. Morgan
questions: A trial court generally has broad discretion when imposing restitution. However, when a victim is paid benefits under the Crime Victims' Compensation Act (CVCA), RCW 9.94.753(7) requires a court to order restitution. Does RCW 9.94A.753 allow a trial court discretion to modify the amount of restitution when ordered for benefits paid under the CVCA?

title: Raab v. Nu Skin Enters., Inc.
questions: Some contracts include a clause that pre-selects a location, or "forum," for resolving future disputes relating to the contract. How does a party seek enforcement of this contractual "forum-selection clause"? What is the proper scope of the court's analysis?

title: Jewels Helping Hands v. Hansen
questions: Are orders on pre-election initiative challenges reviewable? Is this local initiative within the local initiative power?

title: David v. Freedom Vans LLC
questions: RCW 49.62.070 addresses the extent of an employer's authority to restrict low wage employees from accepting outside employment. Employer Freedom Vans required employees David and Springer to sign a noncompete agreement restricting them from directly or indirectly engaging in any business that competed with Freedom Vans. Does Freedom Vans's noncompete agreement violate RCW 49.62.070?

title: Thurman v. Cowles Co.
questions: Does Washington's new anti-SLAPP law, the Uniform Public Expression Act, apply to a defamation claim filed before the Act's effective date but later amended? Does the Uniform Public Expression Act violate the right of access to courts, the right of administration of justice without delay, and the privileges and immunities provision of our constitutions?

title: State v. Mercedes
questions: In this case, animal control officers went to Ms. Mercedes' property to investigate two separate complaints of animal starvation and neglect made by the next-door neighbor. The officers did not have a search warrant. When the officers arrived at the property, they asked Ms. Mercedes to see the animals, which were inside a fenced pasture, and she agreed. Observations gathered while at her property were used to secure a search warrant of the property which led to charges of animal cruelty against Ms. Mercedes. The trial court granted Ms. Mercedes' motion to suppress the evidence and the Court of Appeals reversed. Ms. Mercedes argues that her consent to let the officers see the animals in her pasture was invalid because the officers did not warn her that she could refuse, limit, or later revoke that consent-referred to as Ferrier warnings. Her argument is based on our caselaw that requires law enforcement officers without a search warrant to provide Ferrier warnings when seeking permission to search a person's home for contraband or evidence of a crime. The issue here is whether the officers were required to give Ferrier warnings when they requested permission to search Ms. Mercedes' outdoor property

title: Hall v. Walgreens Boots All., Inc.
questions: Under RCW 19.86.170, is labeling as "non-drowsy" an over-the-counter antitussive containing dextromethorphan hydrobromide an "action[] . . . permitted by . . . [a] regulatory body . . . acting under statutory authority . . . of . . . the United States" such that this labeling decision falls within the statutory safe harbor?

title: City of Wenatchee v. Stearns
questions: Frank Stearns was pulled over for DUI after a citizen's 911 call, an officer's brief contact with the caller on the scene, and the officer's observations of Stearns's driving. Did the officer have reasonable suspicion? 11:00 AM

title: Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Snohomish County v. State
questions: Barry Chrisman was seriously injured when a tree blew down in a windstorm and fell onto his car. The area around the accident site had been recently logged, except for a band of trees in a Riparian Management Zone that were required to be left standing for environmental benefit. The Forest Practices Act immunizes forestland owners when trees required to be left standing in riparian areas blow down and cause damage or injury. Does the Forest Practices Act immunize the defendants in this case? Is immunity dependent on whether the Riparian Management Zone was accurately drawn?

title: Vet Voice Found. v. Hobbs
questions: Washington voters who cast their votes by mail must sign a ballot declaration swearing that they are qualified to vote and have not already voted in the election. Election workers are in turn required to "verify that the voter's signature on the ballot declaration is the same as the signature of that voter in the registration files of the county." RCW 29A.40.110(3). If election workers cannot verify the voter's signature matches one of the signatures on file, they must attempt to contact the voter and give them an opportunity to cure. If the voter does not cure the defect, the ballot is disqualified and will not be counted. Signature verification disproportionally disqualifies the ballots of young people and people of color, among others. Vet Voice and other groups have sued the state, arguing that signature verification facially violates the due process, privileges and immunities, and freedom of elections clauses of our state constitution. The court is asked to decide the proper level of scrutiny that applies to this constitutional challenge and, under that proper scrutiny, whether signature verification is unconstitutional

title: State v. Zghair
questions: A jury convicted Zghair for felony murder by second degree assault. Was the evidence sufficient to prove he either committed the shooting as the principal or was an accomplice?

title: State v. Nelson
questions: Jasper Nelson brings a preenforcement challenge to community custody conditions requiring random breath and urinalysis testing to monitor his compliance with valid conditions prohibiting alcohol and drug use. Nelson argues the testing conditions are unconstitutional because his underlying offenses did not involve alcohol or drugs. Should the court strike the testing conditions?

title: State v. Lewis
questions: Under the Sentencing Reform Act, judges make sentencing decisions based in part on the defendant's "offender score." The offender score is determined by counting "points" for each of the defendant's previous convictions, based on a set of rules under RCW 9.94A.525. At issue in this case is RCW 9.94A.525(3), which says that "out-of- state" convictions can be counted in the offender score. For the purpose of the offender score calculation, do convictions from foreign countries count as "out-of-state" convictions?

title: M.R. v. State
questions: Does Washington's special statute of limitations for bringing claims that stem from injuries suffered as a result of childhood sexual abuse preclude claims of continuing sexual abuse by the same perpetrator that begin at childhood and extend into the victim's adulthood?

title: Cockrum v. C.H. Murphy/Clark-Ullman, Inc.
questions: An employee may sue their employer for workplace injuries under RCW 51.24.020 only if the employer deliberately intended the injury. Are there genuine issues of material fact that Cockrum's employer deliberately intended to cause his mesothelioma?

title: Hous. Auth. v. Knight
questions: Does the CARES Act require 30 days' notice for all evictions or only for nonpayment of rent?

title: State v. J.M.H.
questions: JuCR 7.16 & RCW 13.40.040 address juvenile warrants. Is JuCr 7.16 constitutional? Was this warrant order appealable?

title: State v. Gator's Custom Guns, Inc.
questions: Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill 5078 (ESSB 5078) prohibits the manufacture, distribution, importation, and sale of firearm magazines that can hold more than 10 rounds of ammunition. Does ESSB 5078 violate the right to bear arms protected by article I, section 24 of the Washington Constitution and the Second Amendment of the United States Constitution?

title: Bearden v. City of Ocean Shores
questions: Is a public employee entitled to paid military leave under RCW 38.40.060 if they are not "scheduled to work" by the employer because the employee is on active duty during an extended military leave of absence?

title: State v. Hall-Haught
questions: Were Hall-Haught's confrontation clause rights violated when at her trial forensic test results were admitted into evidence through expert testimony of a surrogate analyst rather than through the testimony of the analyst who conducted the forensic tests?

title: Arends v. State
questions: In Washington, it is illegal for a person to possess a firearm if they were previously convicted of a "serious offense," either in Washington or elsewhere. The law also provides a process for individuals to restore their firearm rights by completing certain statutory requirements. Previously, a person could petition to restore their firearm rights either in their county of residence or the county of their conviction. After July 23, 2023, a person can only petition to restore their firearm rights in the county of their conviction. Arends alleges that he has a vested right to petition for restoration in his county of residence under the former version of the statute because he completed the conditions for firearm restoration prior to July 23, 2023. Does the right to petition to restore firearm rights vest when an individual satisfies the statutory requirements?

title: State v. Bell
questions: This case examines an issue that arose during the jury selection process prior to the actual trial. This process includes attorneys from both parties taking turns questioning prospective jurors to ensure a fair and impartial jury. The parties may ask the court to excuse prospective jurors who show clear bias or undue hardship. The parties may also ask to excuse a limited number of jurors without explanation, referred to as a peremptory challenge. But if a party or court believe the challenge is influenced by racial or ethnic bias, GR 37 requires the challenging party to give a race- neutral explanation. Then, if the court determines an objective observer could view race or ethnicity as a motivating factor, it must deny the challenge. Here, a juror stated he was not paying attention and lost track of the question when asked, "what do you think?". The State used a peremptory challenge against this juror for being inattentive. Mr. Bell raised a GR 37 objection because the juror was the only person of color likely to sit on the jury. The trial court granted the State's peremptory challenge. The issues include the proper standard of review, whether the trial court correctly granted that challenge, and the appropriate remedy

title: Sangha v. Keen
questions: Whether RCW 59.18.365 permits a default judgment against a tenant who appears but does not answer an eviction summons?

title: Erickson v. Pharmacia LLC
questions: Plaintiffs sued Pharmacia, a Missouri corporation, under the Washington Product Liability Act (WPLA). The trial court applied Missouri law that has no statute of repose and allows punitive damages while applying the WPLA as the basis of liability. The court also admitted plaintiffs' expert testimony over Pharmacia's objection. Is Pharmacia entitled to a new trial in light of these rulings?

title: Branson v. Wash. Fine Wine & Spirits, LLC
questions: RCW 49.58.110 requires employers with 15 or more employees to post a position's pay range and benefits in each job posting. RCW 48.58.110(4) provides remedies to a "job applicant or an employee" for violations of this pay transparency requirement, including statutory damages of up to $5,000. In this case, plaintiffs arguably applied to a retailer's online job postings and then sued the retailer, arguing the job postings did not include the required pay and benefit information. Defendant argues plaintiffs are not "job applicants" entitled to the statutory remedy because it alleges they applied for the positions without a good faith or "bona fide" intent to gain employment. The federal district court certified to us the following question: "What must a Plaintiff prove to be deemed a ‘job applicant' within the meaning of RCW 49.58.110(4)? For example, must they prove that they are a ‘bona fide' applicant?"

title: State v. Thompson
questions: Was the defendant's due process rights violated in his appeal when the victim's estate was allowed to intervene to protect the privacy and confidentiality of the victim's medical records?

title: Luv v. W. Coast Servicing, Inc.
questions: West Coast Servicing, Inc. tried to foreclose on Prince Eric Luv's property. However, nine years earlier, a bankruptcy court discharged Luv's personal liability on his debts. The trial court found that West Coast could not initiate foreclosure because the six-year statute of limitations for deeds of trust had already run. After the judgment became final, the Court of Appeals issued Copper Creek (Marysville) Homeowners Ass'n v. Kurtz, 21 Wn. App. 2d 605, 625, 508 P.3d 179 (2022), which contradicted the decision in this case and suggested that West Coast should have been able to initiate foreclosure. West Coast then moved to vacate the judgment under CR 60(b)(11), arguing that there was a change in the law. This case asks us to decide whether the trial court abused its discretion when it determined that these circumstances did not meet the requirements of CR 60(b)(11) to vacate the judgment

title: John Doe P v. Thurston County
questions: Four John Doe plaintiffs brought an action seeking to prevent the release of sex offender records in response to a Public Records Act request. Ultimately, most of the Does' arguments were rejected and most of the records were released. The Does then voluntarily dismissed their case, but requested to remain in pseudonym and continue sealing their actual names in the court record. The issue before this court is whether the Does are entitled to remain anonymous at this post-dismissal stage of the proceedings.

title: Citizen Action Def. Fund v. Off. of Fin. Mgmt.
questions: The Public Records Act requires state agencies to disclose public records upon request, but RCW 42.56.280, the "deliberative process exemption," protects preliminary drafts and other documents that are used to express opinions, recommendations, and formulate policies. That exemption covers documents related to collective bargaining between the State of Washington and employee unions, but the exemption no longer applies and the documents must be disclosed when the "deliberative process" has ended. In this case, the Court has been asked to decide when the "deliberative process" ends during the negotiation of collective bargaining agreements, at which point the records related to the negotiation, such as tentative collective bargaining agreements, are no longer protected by the deliberative process exemption and they must be disclosed

title: In re 365, Attorney at Law
questions: The Washington Public Employees' Association (WPEA) and the State missed the October 1 deadline for submitting tentative collective bargaining agreements for two groups of state employees to the Office of Financial Management for financial feasibility determinations. Is the WPEA entitled to an injunction requiring the State to negotiate toward two-year collective bargaining agreements and to seek legislative funding for both years of the agreements?

title: In re Disciplinary Proceeding Against Wallstrom
questions: The WSBA's Disciplinary Board unanimously recommended that Attorney Wallstrom be disbarred for past financial misconduct, including the knowing and intentional conversion of client funds. Should the Court adopt the Board's recommendation?

title: State v. Luna
questions: Luna was convicted of murder after she stabbed another teenage girl during a fight. To rebut Luna's claim of self defense, the State relied on her statements and demeanor in an interrogation after the fight. Between the interrogation and trial, the legislature enacted RCW 13.40.740, which requires police to provide a juvenile with access to an attorney for consultation before they seek a waiver of the juvenile's constitutional rights and conduct a custodial interrogation. Does RCW 13.40.740 apply such that the evidence of Luna's interrogation should have been excluded?

title: Flying T Ranch, Inc. v. Stillaguamish Tribe of Indians
questions: Does the common law immovable property exception previously applied to foreign nations waive tribal sovereign immunity?

title: In re Pers. Restraint of Schoenhals
questions: Monschke held that the life without parole mandate in RCW 10.95.030 is unconstitutional when applied to 18 to 20-year-old offenders. Is Monschke a "significant change in the law" exemption to the one-year time limit on collateral relief? If so, what must petitioners show to prove they were actually and substantially prejudiced by an earlier decision to obtain collateral relief?

title: State v. Evans
questions: Any person charged with a felony must have their fingerprints, photographs and other identifying information collected. If a person who is charged with a felony appears for their arraignment and they have not been fingerprinted, a court must order that law enforcement do so. In King County, this process is called administrative booking. Kyle Evans appeared for his arraignment at the King County Superior Courthouse, Norm Maleng Regional Justice Center and objected to the County's means of securing his fingerprints. He does not challenge the County's statutory duty to secure his fingerprints but rather challenges the means the County uses to do it. The issue before this court is whether the County's method of taking his fingerprints violates his right to privacy under article I, section 7

title: In re Jr, Attorney at Law
questions: House was convicted of first degree burglary, indecent liberties, second degree assault, and unlawful imprisonment. Did his crimes "require the same criminal intent" so as to "encompass the same criminal conduct" under RCW 9.94A.589(1)(a)?

title: Azorit-Wortham v. Dep't of Lab. & Indus.
questions: A flight attendant filed a workers' compensation claim after contracting COVID-19. The claim was disputed by her employer. The trial court instructed the jury on the traveling employee doctrine, which states that an employee is subject to workers' compensation coverage throughout the duration of a business trip, including during travel, hotel stays, and meals at restaurants. Washington courts have held that the traveling employee doctrine applies when an employee becomes injured during a business trip, but have yet to decide whether the doctrine applies when an employee contracts an illness during a business trip. Does the traveling employee doctrine apply to workers' compensation claims for occupational disease?

title: State v. Balles
questions: This case involves whether this court's decision in State v. Blake, 197 Wn.2d 170, 481 P.3d 521 (2021) immediately invalidated a warrant for Kelly Balles's arrest. In Blake, this court found the statute criminalizing simple drug possession to be unconstitutional. Individuals with convictions based on the statute were entitled to have those convictions vacated, sentences based on those convictions recalculated, and fees paid resulting from those convictions reimbursed. Here, Mr. Balles was serving a community custody sentence for a simple drug possession conviction at the time Blake was published. Prior to the decision, Mr. Balles violated his sentence by failing to report to his corrections officer, resulting in a warrant being issued for his arrest. The warrant was executed after Blake was published, leading to new charges. The issue in this case concerns the validity of that warrant in light of Blake, which indisputably entitled Mr. Balles to have his drug possession conviction vacated and to be released from the remainder of his community custody sentence.

title: State v. Roberts
questions: Is the sufficiency of the evidence test different for bench trials and jury trials? Is the evidence sufficient to support Roberts's conviction for felony murder? Does an offense committed while on Washington supervision for an out-of-state conviction add points to an offender score?

title: Horvath v. DBIA Servs.
questions: The Seattle City Council has created a Parking and Business Improvement Area, the Metropolitan Improvement District, that covers downtown Seattle. The District is supported by assessments imposed on downtown properties. By law, the assessments collected by the city must be spent to benefit the assessed properties. Seattle has chosen a private entity, DBIA Services, to administer the funds. DBIA Services often presents itself as doing business as the District. The Public Records Act applies to the records of state and local agencies, and to private entities that are the functional equivalent of government agencies. Steven Hovarth filed a records request for District records. DBIA Services provided most, but not all, of the records he sought. Specifically, DBIA Services refused to provide salary information for staff whose pay and benefits came from District revenue. When he could not get that information, he sued under the Public Records Act. A trial court decided at summary judgment that DBIA Services was not the functional equivalent of a government agency and thus not subject to the Public Records Act. The court is asked to decide (1) whether the trial court's decision should be reviewed de novo or for abuse of discretion and (2) whether the records are subject to the Public Records Act

title: In re Monro, Attorney at Law
In re Mcminimee, Attorney at Law
State v. Ray
questions: Do the defendant's convictions for second degree assault with a deadly weapon and felony harassment (threat to kill) violate the constitutional rule against double jeopardy? 11:00 AM

title: State v. Danielson
questions: The State violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment when it treats a class of people differently than others who are similarly situated, giving them benefits or burdens based on that classification, without a sufficient state interest to justify that treatment. When a person has been wrongfully convicted, they are entitled to a return of cash paid to satisfy an invalidated conviction. This consolidated case involves two wrongfully-convicted people seeking cash reimbursement for community service work they performed in lieu of paying legal financial obligations (LFOs). A court previously credited this work as payment toward LFOs for their later-invalidated convictions. If the two wrongfully-convicted people were treated differently than others who are similarly situated, based on their membership in a class, what level of scrutiny should a court use to analyze this issue? Is there a sufficient interest for the State to deny them reimbursement for the community service work they performed?

title: State v. Ellis
questions: At a resentencing hearing conducted after our decision in State v. Blake affected the offender score used to calculate Ellis's original sentence, Ellis asked the court to consider the mitigating qualities of his youth at the time of the crime, but the resentencing court told Ellis that youthfulness was "a different issue than the one we're talking about today." Did the resentencing judge abuse its discretion? Ellis also argues his restitution order for $7,097.32 is unconstitutionally excessive. Does Ellis' restitution order violate the excessive fines clauses of the United States and Washington Constitutions?

title: In re Dependency of C.J.J.I.
questions: Does a dependency fact-finding hearing involving an Indian child trigger WICWA's additional procedural protections?

title: In re Feyissa, Attorney at Law
In re Disciplinary Proceeding Against Flood
questions: The Commission on Judicial Conduct censured and recommended the removal of the Bremerton Municipal Court Judge, the Honorable Tracy S. Flood, after accepting Judge Flood's stipulation admitting that she failed to be patient, dignified, and courteous to staff and attorneys, and additionally finding that Judge Flood failed to perform judicial and administrative duties competently and diligently. Should the Court adopt the Commission's recommendation?

title: Galassi v. Lowe's Home Centers, LLC
Dep't of Lab. & Indus. v. Cannabis Green, LLC
